_README: MARKER-ONLY. Never fetched by the student's browser until a teacher/marker PDF is generated (formative: automatically when the student clicks Generate; assessed: only via the ?teacher=1-gated action, after Final Submit). Never render any of this on the student-facing page. See CLAUDE.md section 5's assessment-security amendment.

markingScheme.criterion: Describes the pattern using at least three of the student's own Orbit Lab rows at different eccentricities, quoting actual figures: as eccentricity rose, the closest distance got smaller and the farthest distance got larger (for example e=0.1: 0.90 to 1.10 AU; e=0.5: 0.50 to 1.50 AU; e=0.8: 0.20 to 1.80 AU), and the speed at the closest point rose while the speed at the farthest point fell.
markingScheme.accept: Any three genuine rows from the student's own Investigation Record showing the trend; approximate figures are fine.
markingScheme.insufficient: A general claim ('more elongated orbits are faster at some points') with no recorded figures from at least three of their own Orbit Lab rows.

markingScheme.criterion: States clearly whether the evidence supported or refuted the hypothesis chosen before the experiment, explicitly referencing their own recorded data.
markingScheme.accept: Any judgement (supported / refuted / partially supported) that is consistent with the student's own data and refers back to it.
markingScheme.insufficient: Repeating the hypothesis wording without saying whether the evidence agreed with it.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains why the planet moves faster when closer: the Sun's gravitational pull is stronger when the planet is closer, so the planet is pulled (and accelerated) as it falls toward the Sun, and it slows as it climbs away against that pull.
markingScheme.accept: Equivalent wording such as 'gravity is stronger nearer the Sun so it speeds up'; energy ideas (gravitational potential energy converted to kinetic energy) are also accepted.
markingScheme.insufficient: Stating only that it 'goes faster near the Sun' or 'because it is closer' without linking this to the Sun's gravity.

markingScheme.criterion: States that the Moon's orbit is tilted (by about 5 degrees) relative to the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun, so at most New and Full Moons the Moon passes above or below the Earth-Sun line.
markingScheme.accept: Any equivalent statement that the Moon's orbit is not flat/in the same plane, or that it is 'tilted' or 'inclined'.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying only that the Moon is 'not always lined up' without naming the tilt of its orbit as the reason.

markingScheme.criterion: Correctly describes what must line up for a SOLAR eclipse (the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth at New Moon so its shadow falls on Earth).
markingScheme.accept: Any correct Sun-Moon-Earth order with the Moon in the middle, linked to New Moon.
markingScheme.insufficient: Reversing the order or saying Earth is in the middle for a solar eclipse.

markingScheme.criterion: Correctly describes what must line up for a LUNAR eclipse (Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon at Full Moon so the Moon enters Earth's shadow) and states that eclipses only happen when the alignment is nearly a straight line, which the tilt usually prevents.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct Sun-Earth-Moon order with Earth in the middle, linked to Full Moon, plus the idea that a near-perfect alignment is needed.
markingScheme.insufficient: Describing only one of the two eclipse types, or giving the correct order for lunar without noting the alignment must be nearly exact.

criteria.source: Auto-marked from the Knowledge Check (auto_marked_score, kc1-kc4 = 1 + 4 + 1 + 1 = 7 marks) - the teacher does not mark this row.

= the Explain question's 3-point marking scheme above, one-to-one (pattern from three of their own Orbit Lab rows, hypothesis judgement, gravity-based explanation of speed). Do not award these 3 marks a second time here.

levels.descriptor: None of the three analytic points achieved: no use of own logged orbit rows, no judgement on the hypothesis, and no gravity-based explanation.

Any one of the three analytic points achieved (the pattern quoted from at least three own orbit rows; a supported/refuted judgement tied to the data; or the explanation that stronger gravity nearer the Sun makes the planet faster).
Any two of the three analytic points achieved.

All three analytic points achieved: quotes figures from at least three of their own orbit rows showing the closest/farthest distances and speeds changing with eccentricity; states whether this supported the hypothesis; and explains faster motion when closer in terms of the Sun's stronger gravity.

criteria.source: = the Apply question's 3-point marking scheme above, one-to-one (tilted orbit, solar-eclipse alignment, lunar-eclipse alignment with near-straight-line requirement). Do not award these 3 marks a second time here.

levels.descriptor: None of the three analytic points achieved: no mention of the tilted orbit and no correct alignment described for either eclipse.
Any one of the three analytic points achieved (the Moon's orbit is tilted; correct solar-eclipse alignment; or correct lunar-eclipse alignment with the need for a near-straight line).
Any two of the three analytic points achieved.

All three analytic points achieved: states that the Moon's orbit is tilted so it usually passes above or below the Earth-Sun line; describes the Moon-between alignment for a solar eclipse; and describes the Earth-between alignment for a lunar eclipse with the near-straight-line requirement.

criteria.source: Assessed holistically across both the Explain and Apply answers together - independent of, and never overlapping with, the content marks in use_of_evidence and reasoning above.

levels.descriptor: Too unclear or incomplete for the reasoning to be followed reliably, or key terms (orbit, eccentricity, gravity, eclipse, alignment) are missing or used incorrectly.

Main meaning understandable, but organisation or vocabulary has problems - for example confusing a solar eclipse with a lunar eclipse in wording, or using 'closer' and 'faster' without saying what they refer to.

Clear and logical, using correct vocabulary (orbit, eccentricity, perihelion/aphelion or closest/farthest, gravity, alignment, eclipse) precisely enough to follow easily. Minor spelling or grammar slips do not cost a mark unless they harm meaning.

markingInstructions: Mark ONLY the two constructed responses (Explain, Apply). Award marks point-by-point using each question's markingScheme: each point is worth the marks stated and is independent unless it names a dependsOn point (then it only counts if that point was also met). Accept scientifically valid alternative wording; do not penalise spelling unless meaning is unclear. Check Explain claims against the student's own Investigation Record (Orbit Lab rows) shown in the PDF. The rubric rows use_of_evidence (Explain) and reasoning (Apply) are the same marks as the schemes - do not double count. Knowledge Check is already auto-marked (7 marks). Return: total score, score by criterion, one strength, one correction and one next step in under 80 words.
